{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took on the top line (stroke 1), fetched a tray of 12 dominoes, and laid 14 of them extending the top line outward from the upper-left stretch toward the middle of the fish. That helped the upper outline reach the tail while the bottom line and the supply bin were handled in parallel. The finished fish was fully connected from the start, 113 of 113 dominoes, so the whole outline fell as one run.

Execution: I inspected the table closely seven times, covering the doubled section near the top middle, the nose, and the tail bend. I confirmed the doubled section was one connected run, and I traced the whole run from the start by eye to confirm it carried from nose to both tail points. I also pointed out that the tail bend was too sharp for a simple connect and needed re-laying as a smooth curve. That was the approach we used.

Collaboration: I kept my messages short and specific, and I split the work so that hands stayed apart. I laid from the end of the existing line, away from where others were working, to avoid bumping the table. I gave clear handoffs on who owned the tail, the checks and the supply, and I called a hands-off once the run was verified so nothing was disturbed before the push.

Leadership: I confirmed the plan early, took ownership of the top line, and set up a check-from-the-start routine. I made the call to stop building once the run was verified and to leave the fish untouched. That reduced the risk of late bumps and kept the table calm in the final minutes.

My honest view is that my hands-on building was a modest part of the total, and my main contribution was verification and coordination.", "my_share_percent": 20}
